27902.e: The Law of the Twelve Tables was created around 451 to 450 BC. It is seen as Rome’s oldest written law code.
27902.m: The Law of the Twelve Tables was created around 450 BC.

27903.q: Where were the tablets of the Law of the Twelve Tables put up in public?
27903.e: The tablets stood in the Roman Forum, the centre of public life. This meant every citizen could read the law.
27903.m: The Law of the Twelve Tables was visible to everyone in the Forum.

27904.q: According to tradition, who wrote down the Law of the Twelve Tables?
27904.e: A board of ten men, the decemvirs, was set up to write the laws down. During this time they ruled instead of the consuls.
27904.m: Ten men, the decemvirs, wrote down the Law of the Twelve Tables.

27905.q: Why was the Law of the Twelve Tables so important for the plebeians?
a: The law was now written down and anyone could read it.
27905.e: Before that, it was mainly patrician priests and judges who knew the rules of the law. Written law protected the plebeians better against unfair judgements.
27905.m: Written law protects against arbitrary decisions.

27906.q: According to tradition, which Greek city did Roman envoys visit to study its laws?
27906.e: According to Livy, envoys travelled to Athens to learn about the laws of Solon. Whether this journey really took place is disputed among historians.
27906.m: According to tradition, Athens served as a model for the Law of the Twelve Tables.

27907.q: According to Cicero, what did Roman children have to do with the Law of the Twelve Tables?
27907.e: Cicero reports that boys learned the Law of the Twelve Tables by heart like a set poem. This shows how important it was to the Romans.
27907.m: Roman pupils learned the Law of the Twelve Tables by heart.

27908.q: How were the original tablets of the Law of the Twelve Tables probably lost?
a: When the Gauls invaded Rome around 387 BC
27908.e: It is thought that the tablets were destroyed when the Gauls invaded around 387 BC. Their content is only known from quotations by later writers.
27908.m: We only know the content of the Law of the Twelve Tables from quotations.

27909.q: Who fought against each other in the Punic Wars?
27909.e: Rome and Carthage fought for more than 100 years over control of the western Mediterranean. In the end Rome won.
27909.m: In the Punic Wars, Rome fought Carthage.

27910.q: Where does the word “Punic” come from?
a: From the Latin name for the Phoenicians
From the name of a river in Africa
From the name of a Roman general
27910.e: The Romans called the Carthaginians “Poeni”, meaning Phoenicians. The word “Punic” comes from this.
27910.m: “Punic” comes from the Latin word for the Phoenicians.

27911.q: Which island did Rome and Carthage mainly fight over in the First Punic War?
27911.e: The First Punic War was about control of Sicily. After the victory, the island became the first Roman province.

27912.q: In the First Punic War, what did the Romans first have to build up in order to defeat Carthage?
27912.e: Carthage was a great sea power. So the Romans built many warships in a short time and learned to fight at sea.
27912.m: In the First Punic War, Rome became a sea power.

27913.q: Which of the Punic Wars is also called the “Hannibalic War”?
27913.e: In the Second Punic War (218 to 201 BC), Hannibal led the Carthaginians. That is why it is also called the Hannibalic War.
27913.m: The Second Punic War is also called the Hannibalic War.

27914.q: Who won the First Punic War?
27914.e: After a victory at sea west of Sicily, Rome forced Carthage to make peace in 241 BC. Sicily became Roman.
27914.m: Rome won the First Punic War.

27915.q: How did the Romans at first fight against Hannibal to avoid big defeats?
a: They avoided big battles and only made small attacks
They built a wall across the Alps
27915.e: The general Fabius Maximus avoided open battles. With small attacks he weakened Hannibal’s army, which hardly got any supplies so far from home.
27915.m: Against Hannibal, the Romans at first avoided big battles.

27916.q: What did the Romans do to Carthage in 146 BC at the end of the Third Punic War?
27916.e: After a long siege, the Romans captured Carthage and destroyed it. The area became the Roman province of Africa.
27916.m: In 146 BC the Romans destroyed Carthage.

27917.q: After the peace of 201 BC, what was Carthage no longer allowed to do?
a: Go to war without Rome’s permission
27917.e: Carthage had to give up almost its entire fleet and was no longer allowed to wage war without Rome’s consent. When it defended itself against Numidia anyway, Rome used this as an excuse for a new war.
27917.m: After 201 BC, Carthage needed Rome’s permission for any war.

27918.q: Which city was Carthage’s great rival in ancient times?
27918.e: Rome and Carthage fought three Punic Wars for control of the western Mediterranean. In the end Rome won.
27918.m: Rome and Carthage were bitter rivals.

27919.e: Carthage was founded by Phoenicians from Tyre, a port city in today’s Lebanon. The Phoenicians were famous traders and sailors.
27919.m: Carthage was founded by the Phoenicians.

27922.q: What were the Carthaginians especially well known for?
27922.e: Carthage had a large fleet and traded all over the Mediterranean. Carthaginian sailors even explored the west coast of Africa.
27922.m: The Carthaginians were famous sailors and traders.

27923.q: What does Carthage’s Phoenician name, “Qart-Hadasht”, mean?
27923.e: Qart-Hadasht means “New City”. In Latin this name became “Carthago”.

27924.q: What can still be seen of the city of Carthage today?
a: Ruins from Punic and Roman times
27924.e: After the destruction in 146 BC, the Romans built a new city there. Today you can see ruins from both periods. They are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
27924.m: In Carthage you can see Punic and Roman ruins.

27925.q: Which city did the general Hannibal come from?
27925.e: Hannibal was a general from Carthage in North Africa. His father had already fought against Rome.
27925.m: Hannibal was a general from Carthage.

27926.q: From which region did Hannibal set out on his campaign against Rome?
27926.e: Hannibal started in Spain, where Carthage had bases such as Carthago Nova (today Cartagena). From there he marched over the Pyrenees and the Alps to Italy.
27926.m: Hannibal marched from Spain over the Alps to Italy.

27927.q: In which country did Hannibal fight the Romans for many years after crossing the Alps?
27927.e: After crossing the Alps, Hannibal marched through Italy and defeated the Romans several times. He stayed in Italy for about 15 years but could not conquer Rome.
27927.m: Hannibal fought against Rome in Italy for many years.

27928.q: Which animals did Hannibal take with him on his campaign over the Alps?
27928.e: According to ancient reports, Hannibal marched to Italy with 37 war elephants. Most of them did not survive the harsh winter and the fighting for long.
27928.m: Hannibal crossed the Alps with war elephants.

27929.q: What made Hannibal’s route over the Alps especially dangerous?
a: High waves and storms at sea
27929.e: Hannibal crossed the Alps in autumn. Cold, snow, narrow paths and attacks by mountain peoples cost many soldiers and animals their lives.
27929.m: Hannibal’s crossing of the Alps was very dangerous because of cold and snow.

27930.q: What do we know today about the exact pass Hannibal used?
a: It is marked on a Roman map.
27930.e: Researchers suggest different passes, for example the Col de la Traversette, the Mont Cenis or the Little St Bernard. There is still no clear proof.
27930.m: Exactly which Alpine pass Hannibal took is still unclear.

27931.q: According to Livy, how did Hannibal’s soldiers break up a rock in their way?
a: They heated it with fire and poured vinegar over it.
They had elephants push it away.
They knocked it away with golden hammers.
27931.e: Livy tells how the rock was heated with fire and then doused with vinegar until it crumbled. Whether this is true is not certain.
27931.m: According to Livy, Hannibal broke up a rock with fire and vinegar.

27932.q: Who won the long war between Rome and Hannibal in the end?
27932.e: Hannibal won several times in Italy, but Rome did not give up. In 202 BC Hannibal was defeated in North Africa, and Carthage had to make peace.
27932.m: In the end Rome won the war against Hannibal.

27933.q: Who were the Gracchi in ancient Rome?
27933.e: Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus were brothers from a noble family. As tribunes of the people, both tried to push through reforms.
27933.m: The Gracchi were two brothers who wanted to reform Rome.

27934.q: What did the Gracchi want to achieve for poor farmers in Rome?
a: That they get their own land
27934.e: Many farmers had lost their land, while rich people owned huge estates. The Gracchi wanted to share out state land among poor citizens.
27934.m: The Gracchi wanted to share out land among poor citizens.

27935.q: How were Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus related?
27935.e: Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus were brothers. As politicians in Rome, both stood up for poor citizens. Together they are called the Gracchi.

27936.q: What did Tiberius Gracchus want to achieve with his land law?
a: Share out state land among poor citizens
27936.e: Many small farmers had lost their land, while the rich used large parts of the state land. Tiberius wanted to share out this land again among poor citizens.
27936.m: Tiberius Gracchus wanted to give land back to poor citizens.

27937.q: What did the land law of Tiberius Gracchus aim to limit?
a: How much state land one person could own
How many children a family could have
How many soldiers Rome could have
How much grain people could eat
27937.e: Rich Romans used huge areas of state land. The law limited how much of it one person could have. Anything above that was to be shared out among poor citizens.
27937.m: The land law limited the ownership of state land.

27938.q: How did Tiberius Gracchus meet his end in 133 BC?
a: He was beaten to death by senators and their supporters.
He retired to a country estate.
He fell in a battle against Carthage.
27938.e: Opponents in the Senate accused him of wanting to rule alone. A group of senators and their helpers beat him and many of his supporters to death.
27938.m: Tiberius Gracchus was killed by political opponents.

27939.q: What did a grain law of Gaius Gracchus provide for the citizens of Rome?
27939.e: Gaius Gracchus made sure that citizens in Rome could buy grain at a low, fixed price. This made him very popular with the poor.
27939.m: Gaius Gracchus had grain sold cheaply to citizens.

27940.q: Whose support did the Gracchi mainly rely on for their politics?
27940.e: The Gracchi had their laws passed by the people’s assembly. Many senators were against them because they feared for their property and their power.
27940.m: The Gracchi relied on the ordinary people.

27941.q: Which people did Spartacus come from?
27941.e: Spartacus was a Thracian from the area of today’s Bulgaria. He was taken prisoner and sold as a slave.

27942.q: How did the revolt of Spartacus end?
a: The Romans defeated the army and Spartacus fell
Rome gave all slaves their freedom
27942.e: In 71 BC Crassus defeated the army in southern Italy, and Spartacus fell in battle. Pompey then caught those who fled and also claimed the glory.
27942.m: The revolt of Spartacus was crushed by the Romans.

27943.q: From which city did Spartacus and other gladiators break out in 73 BC?
27943.e: Spartacus and about 70 gladiators escaped from a gladiator school in Capua. With kitchen knives and captured weapons they fought their way free.
27943.m: The revolt of Spartacus began in Capua.

27944.q: Onto which mountain did Spartacus and his people retreat at the start of the revolt?
27944.e: The rebels hid on Vesuvius. According to tradition, they escaped the Romans by climbing down a cliff on ropes made from vines.
27944.m: The rebels gathered around Spartacus on Vesuvius.

27945.q: Roughly how big did Spartacus’ army become?
a: Several tens of thousands of people
27945.e: More and more slaves and poor people joined Spartacus. Ancient sources give figures of 70,000 to over 100,000.
27945.m: Spartacus led an army of several tens of thousands of people.

27946.q: Which Roman general crushed the revolt of Spartacus in 71 BC?
27946.e: Marcus Licinius Crassus defeated the army of Spartacus in southern Italy. Spartacus fell in this battle.
27946.m: Crassus ended the revolt of Spartacus in 71 BC.

27947.q: After the revolt, what happened to about 6000 captured rebels?
a: They were crucified along the Via Appia.
They were sent back to Thrace.
27947.e: As a warning, the prisoners were crucified along the Via Appia between Capua and Rome. This was meant to stop other slaves from rebelling.
27947.m: 6000 rebels were crucified along the Via Appia.

27948.q: What was Marcus Tullius Cicero mainly famous for?
a: As a charioteer in the circus
27948.e: Cicero is seen as the greatest speaker of Rome. His speeches, letters and philosophical writings are still read in Latin lessons today.
27948.m: Cicero was Rome’s most famous speaker.

27949.q: Which high office did Cicero hold in Rome in 63 BC?
27949.e: The consuls were the highest officials of the Roman Republic. There were no emperors yet at that time.

27950.q: What did Cicero uncover as consul?
27950.e: Lucius Sergius Catilina was planning to overthrow the government. Cicero exposed him with famous speeches in the Senate.

27951.q: What does Cicero’s famous cry “O tempora, o mores!” mean?
a: O the times, O the customs!
27951.e: With it, Cicero complained about the decline of morals in Rome. The cry is still quoted today.
27951.m: “O tempora, o mores!” means “O the times, O the customs!”.

27952.q: What was special about Cicero’s rise to the highest office in Rome?
a: Nobody in his family had held a high office before him
He was only twelve years old
He had been a slave before
He was elected by the people of Athens
27952.e: Such a newcomer was called a “homo novus” in Rome, a “new man”. Cicero came from a family of knights from Arpinum.
27952.m: Cicero was the first in his family to hold a high office.

27953.q: After speeches by Demosthenes and Cicero, what is a fierce speech of attack still called today?
27953.e: Demosthenes gave speeches against King Philip, and Cicero used the name for his speeches against Mark Antony. That is where the word “philippic” comes from.
27953.m: A fierce speech of attack is called a philippic.

27954.q: Who had Cicero killed in 43 BC?
27954.e: Mark Antony put Cicero on the list of enemies of the state. Soldiers killed him as he tried to flee.
27954.m: Cicero was killed on the orders of Mark Antony.

27955.q: Which title of honour did Cicero receive after saving Rome from a conspiracy?
27955.e: After the conspiracy of Catilina was crushed, Cicero was called “pater patriae”, Father of the Fatherland. Later the emperors also bore this title.
27955.m: Cicero was called “Father of the Fatherland”.

27956.q: Which three men formed the First Triumvirate?
27956.e: Caesar, Pompey and Crassus made a secret alliance. Together they pushed through their interests against the Senate.
27956.m: The First Triumvirate was made up of Caesar, Pompey and Crassus.

27957.q: What did Caesar, Pompey and Crassus want to achieve with their alliance?
a: To push through their aims against the Senate
To give the slaves their freedom
27957.e: The three powerful men helped one another. In this way, from 60 BC they pushed through their interests against the Senate.
27957.m: The First Triumvirate helped three men get their way against the Senate.

27958.e: The word comes from the Latin “tres viri”, three men. It means an alliance or office held by three people.
27958.m: A triumvirate is an alliance of three men.

27959.q: How did Pompey strengthen his alliance with Caesar?
27959.e: In 59 BC Pompey married Caesar’s daughter Julia. Her death in 54 BC weakened the bond between the two men.
27959.m: A marriage closely linked Pompey with Caesar.

27960.q: What was the First Triumvirate in Rome?
a: An alliance of three powerful politicians
27960.e: Caesar, Pompey and Crassus formed an alliance in 60 BC. In 56 BC they renewed it in the town of Luca.
27960.m: The First Triumvirate was an alliance of three politicians.

27961.q: What brought the First Triumvirate to an end in 53 BC?
27961.e: Crassus wanted to win glory in the East and fell fighting against the Parthians. After that, only Caesar and Pompey faced each other.
27961.m: With the death of Crassus, the First Triumvirate fell apart.

27962.q: What was Marcus Licinius Crassus especially well known for in Rome?
27962.e: Crassus was thought to be the richest man in Rome. Among other things, he made money from land and houses in the city.
27962.m: Crassus was the richest man in ancient Rome.

a: A small river in northern Italy
27963.e: The Rubicon is a small river in north-eastern Italy. In the Roman Republic it was an important border.
27963.m: The Rubicon is a small river in northern Italy.

27964.q: Which Roman general crossed the Rubicon with his soldiers in 49 BC?
27964.e: Caesar came from Gaul with his troops. Crossing the Rubicon started a civil war in Rome.
27964.m: Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC.

27965.q: Into which sea does the Rubicon flow?
27965.e: The Rubicon flows north of Rimini and into the Adriatic. For a long time it was disputed exactly where the ancient Rubicon ran.
27965.m: The Rubicon flows into the Adriatic.

27966.q: According to ancient sources, with how many legions did Caesar cross the Rubicon?
27966.e: Caesar only had the 13th Legion with him. His other troops were still in Gaul, but he still dared to advance quickly.
27966.m: Caesar dared to cross the Rubicon with just one legion.

27967.q: Why was crossing the Rubicon with troops such a serious act?
a: A governor was not allowed to march into Italy with his army.
The river was thought to be the home of the gods.
It was the border with the Parthian Empire.
Bridges over the Rubicon were forbidden.
27967.e: A general had to leave his army behind at the border of his province. Anyone who entered Italy with an army was practically declaring war on the state.
27967.m: Crossing the Rubicon with an army meant civil war.

27968.q: What does the saying “to cross the Rubicon” mean today?
a: To make a decision that cannot be undone
To set off on a journey abroad
To only just pass an exam
27968.e: Someone who crosses the Rubicon makes a decision with no way back. The saying recalls Caesar’s decision.
27968.m: Once you cross the Rubicon, there is no going back.

27969.q: Who was Caesar’s great opponent in the civil war after the Rubicon?
27969.e: Pompey had once been Caesar’s ally. In the civil war Caesar defeated him in 48 BC, after which Pompey fled to Egypt.
27969.m: In the civil war, Caesar defeated Pompey.

27970.q: Which day is meant by the “Ides of March”?
27970.e: The Romans called the middle of the month the Ides. In March this was the 15th day. On this day in 44 BC Caesar was murdered.
27970.m: The Ides of March are 15 March.

27971.q: What did the conspirators want to celebrate with a coin after Caesar’s murder?
27971.e: One of the conspirators had a coin made showing two daggers and a cap of liberty. It presented the murder as freeing Rome from a sole ruler.
27971.m: The conspirators celebrated Caesar’s murder as the liberation of Rome.

27972.q: What did the Roman state declare Caesar to be after his death?
27972.e: After his death, Caesar was officially declared a god. Later a temple was built for him in the Forum.
27972.m: Caesar was declared a god after his death.

a: At a meeting of the Senate in the Curia of Pompey
In his house on the Palatine
On a boat on the Tiber
27973.e: The Senate meeting took place in a hall next to the Theatre of Pompey. Caesar is said to have died at the foot of a statue of Pompey.
27973.m: Caesar was stabbed during a meeting of the Senate.

27974.q: What did the conspirators kill Caesar with?
27974.e: The conspirators hid daggers under their robes. At the Senate meeting they stabbed Caesar.

27975.q: Which title had Caesar taken shortly before his murder?
a: Tribune of the people for ever
27975.e: At the beginning of 44 BC Caesar became dictator for life. Many senators feared that he wanted to rule like a king.
27975.m: As dictator for life, Caesar seemed like a king to many senators.

27976.q: According to tradition, who warned Caesar about the Ides of March?
27976.e: The seer Spurinna is said to have warned Caesar of a danger that would come by the Ides of March at the latest. In Shakespeare the line is “Beware the Ides of March”.
27976.m: A seer warned Caesar about the Ides of March.

27977.q: After Caesar’s death, who finally became sole ruler and the first emperor of Rome?
27977.e: Caesar’s adopted son Octavian defeated his opponents and ruled alone from 27 BC. He called himself Augustus and is seen as the first Roman emperor.
27977.m: After Caesar, Augustus became the first emperor of Rome.

27978.q: In which year AD was Pompeii destroyed by a volcanic eruption?
27978.e: In AD 79 Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii under a thick layer of ash and pumice.

27979.q: Which natural event had already badly damaged Pompeii about 17 years before the volcanic eruption?
27979.e: Around AD 62 a strong earthquake shook the area. Many buildings were still being repaired when the city was buried.
27979.m: Even before the eruption, an earthquake had badly damaged Pompeii.

27980.q: Near which modern large city is Pompeii?
27980.e: Pompeii lies in Campania in southern Italy, about 25 kilometres south-east of Naples.

27983.q: How did archaeologists make the body shapes of the victims of Pompeii visible again?
a: They poured plaster into hollow spaces
They built figures out of wood
27983.e: The bodies decayed in the ash and left hollow spaces. From 1863 Giuseppe Fiorelli had these filled with plaster.
27983.m: The plaster casts show the shapes of the victims of Pompeii.

27984.q: Why is Pompeii still so well preserved today?
a: It was repaired again and again
27984.e: The layer of ash and pumice, several metres thick, protected houses, wall paintings and everyday objects for almost 1700 years.
27984.m: Under ash and pumice, Pompeii stayed almost unchanged.

27985.q: What can visitors see in Pompeii today?
a: Roman streets, houses and wall paintings
An active lava lake in the middle of the town
27985.e: Archaeologists have dug up a large part of the city. You can walk through old streets and look at houses, bakeries and wall paintings.
27985.m: In Pompeii you can visit a Roman town.

27987.q: Apart from gladiator fights, what else was shown in the Colosseum?
27987.e: In animal hunts, people fought against lions, bears and other wild animals. Chariot races, on the other hand, took place in the Circus Maximus.
27987.m: There were also fights with wild animals in the Colosseum.

27988.q: Where does the Colosseum probably get its name from?
a: From a huge statue next to it
27988.e: Next to the building stood a huge statue, the Colossus of Nero. Later the amphitheatre was named the Colosseum after it.
27988.m: The Colosseum is named after a huge statue.

27989.q: Roughly how high is the outer wall of the Colosseum?
27989.e: The Colosseum is about 48 metres high, 188 metres long and 156 metres wide. It was the largest amphitheatre in the Roman Empire.
27989.m: The wall of the Colosseum is about 50 metres high.

27990.q: What were the fighters called who fought each other in front of an audience in the Colosseum?
27990.e: Gladiators were mostly slaves, prisoners of war or condemned criminals who were trained for the fights in special schools.

27991.q: How were the spectators in the Colosseum protected from the sun?
27991.e: Sailors stretched huge lengths of cloth above the seats. This awning was called the velarium.
27991.m: An awning protected the spectators in the Colosseum.

27992.q: What was underneath the arena of the Colosseum?
a: Passages and cages for animals and fighters
A water tank for the whole of Rome
27992.e: Animals and fighters waited under the arena. With lifts and trapdoors they appeared in the arena by surprise.
27992.m: Under the arena there were passages, cages and lifts.

27993.q: How did the large amount of water get into the big baths in the city of Rome?
27993.e: Aqueducts carried fresh spring water into the city on a gentle slope, often over many kilometres. Part of it supplied the baths.
27993.m: Aqueducts brought the water to the baths.

27994.q: What was the room with the cold bath in the Roman baths called?
27994.e: The word comes from the Latin “frigidus”, meaning cold. People cooled off there after sweating.
27994.m: In the frigidarium you took a cold bath.

27995.q: What is the Roman underfloor heating that heated the baths called?
27995.e: Under the floor, resting on small brick pillars, hot air flowed from a furnace and warmed the floor and walls.
27995.m: The hypocaust was a Roman underfloor heating system.

27996.q: How big were the Baths of Caracalla in Rome?
a: Huge, over a thousand people could bathe at the same time
Just one pool for ten people
Just big enough for the emperor alone
27996.e: The Baths of Caracalla were finished around AD 216. There was room for over a thousand bathers at the same time. Today the ruins are used as an opera stage in summer.
27996.m: The Baths of Caracalla were a huge bathing complex.

27997.q: Where did visitors to the Roman baths put their clothes?
a: In niches in the wall of the changing room
Nowhere, they bathed in their clothes
27997.e: In the changing room, the apodyterium, there were niches in the walls for clothes. Often a slave kept watch so that nothing was stolen.
27997.m: In the changing room the Romans put their clothes in wall niches.

27998.q: What did the Romans use a strigil for in the baths?
a: To scrape off oil and sweat
27998.e: Soap was hardly known. People rubbed themselves with oil and scraped it off again, along with the dirt, using the curved metal scraper.
27998.m: The strigil was used to clean the skin.

27999.q: What was the palaestra in a Roman bath used for?
27999.e: The palaestra was an open courtyard where people could wrestle, run or play ball before bathing.
27999.m: In the palaestra people did sport before bathing.

28000.q: What do you mainly see in the Roman Forum today?
28000.e: Columns, arches and remains of walls survive from what was once the centre of Rome. Many tourists visit the ruins.
28000.m: Today there are ruins in the Roman Forum.

28001.q: The Roman Forum lies in a hollow between hills. On how many hills is ancient Rome said to have been built?
28001.e: Rome is also called the “City of Seven Hills”. The Forum lies between two of them, the Capitol and the Palatine.
28001.m: Rome is the city of seven hills.

28002.q: What were the large halls in the Roman Forum called, where trials were held and business was done?
28002.e: Well-known examples are the Basilica Julia and the Basilica Aemilia. Later, Christian churches took over this type of building.
28002.m: Justice was done in the basilica at the Forum.

28003.q: What was the Roman Forum in ancient Rome?
a: The most important square in the city
28003.e: In the Forum the Romans met to trade, for courts, speeches and festivals. Temples and halls stood all around it.
28003.m: The Roman Forum was the centre of ancient Rome.

29674.q: In which year did the Helvetii set off from the Swiss Plateau to emigrate to Gaul?
29674.e: In spring 58 BC the Helvetii left their land with allied tribes. Julius Caesar stood in their way.
29674.m: The departure of the Helvetii began in 58 BC.

29675.q: According to Caesar, which rich Helvetian nobleman planned the departure of the Helvetii?
29675.e: Orgetorix persuaded the Helvetii to emigrate. But he died in 60 BC, before the march even began.
29675.m: Orgetorix planned the departure of the Helvetii.

29676.q: According to Caesar, what did the Helvetii do with their towns and villages before they set off?
a: They gave them to the Raetians
29676.e: Caesar reports that they burned their 12 towns and about 400 villages. That way nobody would think of turning back.
29676.m: Before setting off, the Helvetii burned their own settlements.

29677.q: Where did the Helvetii want to go in the year they left?
a: To south-west Gaul by the Atlantic
To northern Italy in the Po valley
29677.e: Their goal was the land of the Santones in the south-west of present-day France. There they hoped for more land and safety.
29677.m: The Helvetii wanted to settle in western Gaul near the Atlantic.

29678.q: Whose account gives us most of what we know about the departure of the Helvetii?
29678.e: Caesar described the campaign himself in his work “De bello Gallico” (The Gallic War). Because he took part in the war himself, his account is not neutral.
29678.m: Julius Caesar is the most important source on the departure of the Helvetii.

29679.q: At which town did Caesar have the bridge over the Rhône destroyed to block the Helvetii’s way?
29679.e: Geneva then belonged to the Allobroges and already lay within Roman power. Caesar had the bridge torn down and the bank of the Rhône fortified.
29679.m: Caesar blocked the Helvetii’s way across the Rhône at Geneva.

29680.q: According to Caesar, how many people set off in total with the Helvetii and their allies?
29680.e: Caesar gives 368,000 people, about 92,000 of them warriors. Experts today think this number is exaggerated.
29680.m: According to Caesar, several hundred thousand people set off with the Helvetii.

29681.q: Why did Caesar force the defeated Helvetii to return to their old homeland?
a: So that no Germanic tribes would take the empty land
So that they would mine gold there for Rome
Because the Romans did not know the land
Because a war against Raetia was starting there
29681.e: An empty Swiss Plateau would have attracted Germanic tribes from across the Rhine. The Helvetii were to act as a buffer and rebuild their settlements.
29681.m: The Helvetii had to return so that their land would not fall into Germanic hands.

29682.q: In which present-day country is the site of the Battle of Bibracte?
29682.e: Bibracte lay in what is now the region of Burgundy in France. So the Helvetii were already far from their homeland.
29682.m: The Battle of Bibracte took place in present-day France.

29683.q: Who won the Battle of Bibracte?
29683.e: Caesar’s legions defeated the Helvetii after a long, hard fight. That meant the departure had failed.
29683.m: At Bibracte the Romans under Caesar defeated the Helvetii.

29684.q: Which people from the area of present-day Switzerland were defeated at Bibracte?
29684.e: The Helvetii had emigrated in 58 BC. At Bibracte they were defeated by Caesar.
29684.m: At Bibracte the Helvetii were defeated by the Romans.

29685.q: Why did the Helvetii leave their homeland before the Battle of Bibracte?
a: They were looking for new, better land
A volcano had destroyed their land
They wanted to sail across the sea
29685.e: The Helvetii wanted to move to western Gaul, where they hoped for more space. Caesar stood in their way.
29685.m: The Helvetii set off to find new land.

29686.e: Oppida were large Celtic settlements protected by ramparts and walls. Caesar used this Latin word for them.
29686.m: An oppidum is a fortified Celtic town.

29687.q: What did the Helvetii have to do after their defeat at Bibracte?
29687.e: Caesar sent the survivors back to their homeland. There they were to rebuild their destroyed villages.
29687.m: After Bibracte the Helvetii had to go home.

29688.q: What did the Helvetii do with their villages before they left?
a: They sold them to the Romans
They gave them to the Germanic tribes
29688.e: According to Caesar the Helvetii burned down their towns and villages. That way there was no going back for them.
29688.m: Before leaving, the Helvetii burned down their villages.

29689.e: A villa rustica was a farm with a house, stables and storehouses. There were hundreds of them on the Swiss Plateau.
29689.m: A villa rustica was a Roman farm in the countryside.

29690.q: What belonged to a villa rustica?
29690.e: A villa rustica was a Roman farm. Besides the owner’s house there were stables, workshops and storehouses.
29690.m: A villa rustica was a Roman farm with many buildings.

29691.q: How were some rooms heated in grand Roman country estates?
29691.e: In hypocaust heating, hot air from a fire flowed under the floor and through the walls. For this the floor rested on small brick pillars.
29691.m: The Romans heated rooms with underfloor heating, the hypocaust.

29692.q: What did Roman country estates in Switzerland mainly produce?
29692.e: The estates grew grain and kept livestock. They sold what they did not need to towns and to the army.
29692.m: Roman country estates mainly supplied the land with food.

29693.q: What is the Roman country estate of Orbe-Boscéaz in the canton of Vaud especially famous for?
29693.e: Several magnificent mosaic floors survive at Orbe-Boscéaz. They show gods and animals, for example.
29693.m: The estate at Orbe is famous for its beautiful mosaics.

29694.q: What were the roofs of Roman country estates usually covered with?
29694.e: The Romans brought roof tiles of fired clay to our region. Flat tiles and round curved tiles were used together.
29694.m: Roman country estates had roofs of fired tiles.

29695.q: What hit many Roman country estates in Switzerland hard from the middle of the 3rd century?
a: A volcanic eruption in the Jura
29695.e: Around AD 260 the Alemanni pushed across the Rhine and plundered. Many estates got destroyed or abandoned.
29695.m: Germanic raids brought many estates to an end.

29696.q: Which people lived in the alpine valleys of present-day Grisons before the Romans?
29696.e: The Raetians were an alpine people with their own language and script. The Roman province was named after them.
29696.m: The Raetians lived in the Grisons before Roman times.

29697.q: In which year did the Romans conquer the Raetians in a great alpine campaign?
29697.e: Emperor Augustus wanted to secure the alpine passes. In 15 BC his troops conquered the alpine region as far as the Danube.
29697.m: The Roman alpine campaign took place in 15 BC.

29698.q: Which Roman emperor had the alpine peoples conquered in 15 BC?
29698.e: Emperor Augustus wanted to secure the alpine passes. His stepsons led the campaign against the Raetians.
29698.m: Emperor Augustus had the Alps conquered.

29699.q: Which people was the Roman province of Raetia named after?
29699.e: The Raetians lived in the alpine valleys. The Romans named the new province after them.
29699.m: Raetia is named after the Raetians.

29700.q: Which Swiss national language goes back to the everyday Latin of the province of Raetia?
29700.e: The people took on the Latin of the Romans. Over centuries this developed into Romansh in the Grisons.
29700.m: Romansh developed from the Latin of the province of Raetia.

29701.q: Which town in the Grisons was already important in Roman times and was then called Curia?
29701.e: Chur is one of the oldest towns in Switzerland. In late antiquity it served as the capital of a Roman province and later became the seat of a bishop.

29702.q: What did the Romans build to celebrate their victory over the alpine peoples?
29702.e: The victory monument Tropaeum Alpium stands in La Turbie near Monaco. Its inscription names 46 conquered alpine peoples.
29702.m: A Roman victory monument recalls the conquest of the Alps.

29703.q: Lousonna is the Roman settlement that came before which present-day city?
29703.e: The name Lousonna is recorded in inscriptions. The present-day place name Lausanne developed from it.
29703.m: The name Lausanne came from the Roman Lousonna.

29704.q: Which language did the Romans speak in Lousonna?
29704.e: In Roman times Latin served as the language of government and trade. French later developed from everyday Latin.
29704.m: In Roman times people in Lousonna spoke Latin.

29705.q: On which lake did the Roman settlement of Lousonna lie?
29705.e: Lousonna lay right on the northern shore of Lake Geneva. Its position by the water was very good for trade.
29705.m: Lousonna was a Roman settlement on Lake Geneva.

29706.q: What did Lousonna have right on the lake shore?
29706.e: There was a harbour on the shore. An inscription by boatmen shows that goods were transported by water.
29706.m: Lousonna had a harbour for trade.

29707.q: What kind of settlement was Lousonna in Roman times?
a: A small town with a harbour
29707.e: Lousonna, a Roman vicus on Lake Geneva, had a harbour, a market and temples. A few thousand people lived there.
29707.m: Lousonna: a small Roman town on the lake.

29708.q: Where did the settlement move to when things became unsafe from the late 3rd century?
a: To an island in the lake
Into the Rhône valley to Sion
29708.e: Because of Germanic raids, people moved further up to a safe place. This became the medieval bishop’s town of Lausanne.
29708.m: For safety, the people of Lousonna moved up onto the hill.

29709.q: Which international organisation has its headquarters today on the site of the former Lousonna?
29709.e: The IOC headquarters, Olympic House, stands in Vidy. Parts of the Roman settlement used to lie there.
29709.m: The International Olympic Committee is based on the ground of old Lousonna.

29710.q: Which two areas does the Great St Bernard Pass connect?
29710.e: The pass road leads from the Rhône valley through the Val d’Entremont over into the Italian Aosta Valley. The Romans already used this route to Gaul.
29710.m: The Great St Bernard connects Valais with the Aosta Valley.

29711.q: Roughly how high is the top of the Great St Bernard Pass?
29711.e: The top of the pass is 2,469 metres above sea level. In winter the road is closed because of snow.
29711.m: The Great St Bernard is almost 2,500 metres high.

29712.q: Which people built a road for vehicles over the Great St Bernard almost 2,000 years ago?
29712.e: Before that you could only cross the pass with pack animals. In the 1st century AD the Romans widened the road for carts.
29712.m: The Romans made the Great St Bernard passable for vehicles.

29713.q: To which chief Roman god was the temple at the top of the Great St Bernard Pass dedicated?
29713.e: The Celts worshipped the god Poeninus on the pass. The Romans linked him with their chief god Jupiter.
29713.m: At the top of the pass stood a Roman temple to Jupiter.

29714.q: Which town in Valais at the foot of the Great St Bernard was an important place with an amphitheatre in Roman times?
29714.e: Martigny counted as the most important Roman place in Valais. An amphitheatre and the remains of a temple still survive there.
29714.m: Martigny: the main Roman town at the foot of the Great St Bernard.

29715.q: Which town on the south side of the pass was called Augusta Praetoria in Roman times?
29715.e: Augusta Praetoria got founded around 25 BC. The name Aosta developed from “Augusta”.
29715.m: Aosta: the Roman town at the southern foot of the Great St Bernard.

29716.q: What were the stone pillars called that showed distances along Roman roads like the one over the Great St Bernard?
29716.e: Milestones gave the distance to the next important place and often the emperor’s name. Some stand in museums today.
29716.m: Milestones showed distances along Roman roads.

29717.q: When did the Alemanni begin to settle permanently on the Swiss Plateau?
29717.e: After the end of Roman rule, the Alemanni gradually moved across the Rhine. They settled first in northern Switzerland and then further south.
29717.m: The Alemanni settled the Swiss Plateau in the 5th and 6th centuries.

29718.q: Which place-name ending is typical of early Alemannic settlements in German-speaking Switzerland?
29718.e: The ending means something like “among the people of ...” and points to a clan. Examples are Ossingen, Beringen and Hettlingen.
29718.m: The ending -ingen often reveals an early Alemannic settlement.

29719.q: Which group of dialects does Swiss German belong to?
29719.e: The dialects of German-speaking Switzerland go back to the language of the Alemanni. People in Alsace and southern Baden also speak Alemannic.
29719.m: Swiss German is an Alemannic dialect.

29720.q: Which people did the Alemanni have to submit to around AD 500?
29720.e: The Frankish king Clovis defeated the Alemanni in several battles. After that their land belonged to the Frankish kingdom.
29720.m: Around 500 the Alemanni came under Frankish rule.

29721.q: What happened when the Romans withdrew many soldiers from the Rhine border around AD 400?
a: The Alemanni moved more easily into northern Switzerland
The Vikings occupied the Swiss Plateau
29721.e: The Romans needed the soldiers to defend Italy. After that the way across the Rhine lay more open for the Alemanni.
29721.m: After the Romans withdrew, the Alemanni came to northern Switzerland.

29722.q: What religion did the Alemanni have when they settled in northern Switzerland?
29722.e: At first the Alemanni worshipped Germanic gods such as Woden. Only in the 7th and 8th centuries did they gradually become Christians.
29722.m: The early Alemanni believed in Germanic gods.

29723.q: Which finds tell archaeologists most about the early Alemanni in Switzerland?
29723.e: The Alemanni buried their dead in rows of graves with weapons, jewellery and tools. These grave goods show how they lived.
29723.m: Alemannic cemeteries are an important source for the early Middle Ages.

29724.q: Which Germanic people settled in what is now western Switzerland in the 5th century?
29724.e: In 443 the Romans gave the Burgundians land in Sapaudia, in present-day western Switzerland and Savoy. They were meant to protect the border there.
29724.m: The Burgundians settled in western Switzerland in the 5th century.

29725.q: Which area belonged to the Kingdom of Upper Burgundy, founded in 888?
a: Large parts of present-day western Switzerland
29725.e: Rudolph I had himself crowned in 888 in the Abbey of Saint-Maurice. His kingdom covered large parts of present-day western Switzerland.
29725.m: The Kingdom of Upper Burgundy lay in present-day western Switzerland.

29726.q: What did the Burgundian king Gundobad have written down around AD 500?
29726.e: The law of the Burgundians is called the Lex Burgundionum. It set out how Burgundians and Romans lived together.
29726.m: King Gundobad had the law of the Burgundians written down.

29727.q: What happened to the language of the Burgundians in western Switzerland?
a: They took on the Latin of the locals
They spread their Germanic language everywhere
They took on the Raetian language
29727.e: The Burgundians were few and lived among many Romanised locals. They gave up their Germanic language; the French of Romandy later developed from this.
29727.m: The Burgundians adapted and soon spoke a Romance language.

29728.q: Which people conquered the first kingdom of the Burgundians in 534?
29728.e: The sons of Clovis defeated the Burgundians and made their kingdom part of the Frankish kingdom. But the name Burgundy remained.
29728.m: In 534 the Burgundian kingdom fell to the Franks.

29729.q: How does the Burgundian Queen Bertha live on in the legends of western Switzerland?
29729.e: Queen Bertha married King Rudolph II. The saying “au temps où la reine Berthe filait” (in the days when Queen Bertha spun) recalls her as the good old days.
29729.m: Queen Bertha is a popular legendary figure in Romandy.

29730.q: Which empire did Burgundy belong to after the death of King Rudolph III in 1032?
29730.e: After Rudolph III died, the German Emperor Conrad II took over the Kingdom of Burgundy. So western Switzerland also belonged to the Empire.
29730.m: From 1032 Burgundy belonged to the Holy Roman Empire.

29731.q: Which river is seen as the symbol of the German-French language border in Switzerland?
29731.e: The Saane (in French Sarine) flows through the canton of Fribourg. It symbolically separates German-speaking Switzerland from Romandy.
29731.m: The Saane stands as a symbol of the language border.

29732.q: What is the border between German-speaking Switzerland and Romandy jokingly called?
29732.e: The term means “rösti ditch” and refers to rösti, which is seen as typical of German-speaking Switzerland. People often use it when the two parts of the country vote differently.
29732.m: The language border is jokingly called the Röstigraben.

29733.q: Which Swiss town is officially bilingual in German and French?
29733.e: In Biel/Bienne, street signs, authorities and schools are bilingual. Many people switch between the two languages in everyday life.
29733.m: Biel/Bienne is the largest bilingual town in Switzerland.

29734.q: How many Swiss cantons are officially bilingual in German and French?
29734.e: They are the cantons of Bern, Fribourg and Valais. The Grisons is trilingual, with German, Romansh and Italian.
29734.m: Bern, Fribourg and Valais are bilingual cantons.

29735.q: In which part of Valais do most people speak French?
29735.e: In the lower, western part of Valais people mainly speak French. In Upper Valais, which includes the Goms and the Saas valley, people speak German.
29735.m: In Lower Valais people speak French, in Upper Valais German.

29736.q: How did the German-French language border in Switzerland come about?
29736.e: In the early Middle Ages the language of the Alemanni spread, while in the west people spoke a Romance language. So the border gradually took shape.
29736.m: The language border grew over centuries.

29737.q: Which small town in the canton of Fribourg is mainly German-speaking?
29737.e: Murten (in French Morat) lies close to the language border. Most of its people speak German.
29737.m: Murten is a German-speaking town in the bilingual canton of Fribourg.

29738.q: On which day is St Gall’s Day celebrated?
29738.e: St Gall’s Day marks the day the saint died. In the past it was an important date in the countryside, for example for markets and paying interest.
29738.m: St Gall’s Day is on 16 October.

29739.q: According to tradition, which country did the monk Gallus come from?
29739.e: According to tradition Gallus came from Ireland. As a monk he travelled through France as far as Lake Constance.
29739.m: According to tradition Gallus came from Ireland.

29740.q: How did Gallus live in the area of present-day St Gallen?
a: As a hermit in a cell in the forest
As a king in a castle
As a trader in a town
As a farmer on a big farm
29740.e: Gallus built himself a simple cell in the forest and lived there as a hermit. The town of St Gallen later grew from this place.
29740.m: Gallus lived as a hermit in the forest.

29741.q: According to tradition, how did Columbanus and Gallus deal with the pagan idols of the Alemanni?
a: They put them up in churches
29741.e: The accounts of their lives report that Gallus destroyed idols in Tuggen and Bregenz or threw them into the lake. This turned the locals against the monks.
29741.m: Gallus fought against the old Alemannic belief in gods.

29742.q: According to legend, which animal brought Gallus wood while he was building his cell?
29742.e: Gallus is said to have told the animal to put wood on the fire and given it bread in return. That is why the coat of arms of the city of St Gallen shows this animal.
29742.m: According to legend a bear helped St Gallus.

29743.q: What was founded at the grave of Gallus in 719?
29743.e: The priest Otmar founded a monastery at the grave of Gallus. The town of St Gallen later grew up around the monastery.
29743.m: The Abbey of St Gall grew up at the grave of Gallus.

29744.q: What in St Gallen is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
a: The Abbey District with cathedral and library
29744.e: The Abbey District is the former monastery of Gallus. With the cathedral and the famous Abbey Library, it has been a World Heritage Site since 1983.
29744.m: The Abbey District of St Gallen is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

29745.q: Who ruled large areas of present-day eastern Switzerland from the Abbey of St Gall until 1798?
29745.e: The abbot of St Gall also ruled as a worldly lord. That is why he was called the Prince-Abbot. In 1805 the monastery was dissolved.
29745.m: The Prince-Abbot of St Gall ruled over large parts of eastern Switzerland.

29746.q: Which building on the Plan of St Gall is drawn largest and most precisely?
29746.e: The church forms the centre of the whole complex. It is drawn especially carefully, with altars and measurements.
29746.m: The great church stands at the centre of the monastery plan.

29747.q: Around which year was the Plan of St Gall made?
29747.e: Experts date the plan to about 819 to 837, usually around 825/826. So it comes from the Carolingian period.
29747.m: The monastery plan comes from the early 9th century.

29748.q: What material is the Plan of St Gall drawn on?
29748.e: The plan consists of five pieces of parchment, that is treated animal skin, sewn together. It measures about 112 by 77 centimetres.
29748.m: The monastery plan is drawn on parchment.

29749.q: Roughly how many buildings are drawn on the Plan of St Gall?
29749.e: The plan contains floor plans of about 50 buildings with 333 labels. The complex would have had room for over 100 monks.
29749.m: About fifty buildings can be seen on the monastery plan.

29750.q: How is the cemetery designed on the Plan of St Gall?
29750.e: Fruit trees are drawn between the graves. In this way the plan links the place of the dead with a picture of the garden of paradise.
29750.m: On the monastery plan the cemetery is also an orchard.

29751.q: What was the Plan of St Gall meant for?
a: As a model for an ideal monastery
As a map of eastern Switzerland
As a plan for building a castle
As a street map of St Gallen
29751.e: The plan shows what a perfect monastery with a church, workshops, gardens and stables could look like. But it was never built exactly like this.
29751.m: The monastery plan shows an ideal monastery.

29752.q: Roughly how old is the Abbey of Saint-Maurice in Valais?
29752.e: The abbey was founded in 515. In 2015 it celebrated 1,500 years.
29752.m: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice is over 1,500 years old.

29753.q: In which canton is the Abbey of Saint-Maurice?
29753.e: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice lies in the Rhône valley in the canton of Valais. It was founded in 515.
29753.m: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice is in Valais.

29754.q: Which saint is the Abbey of Saint-Maurice named after?
29754.e: Maurice and his soldiers are said to have died as martyrs here. The French name Maurice comes from the Latin Mauritius.
29754.m: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice bears the name of St Maurice.

29755.q: According to the legend of Saint-Maurice, who was St Maurice?
29755.e: According to legend, Maurice led a Roman troop. He and his soldiers are said to have been killed because, as Christians, they would not obey.
29755.m: According to legend, Maurice was a Roman soldier and a Christian.

29756.q: Who had a post at Saint-Maurice long before the monastery?
29756.e: The Romans had a customs and military post here at a narrow point in the Rhône valley. The place was called Agaunum then.
29756.m: Saint-Maurice was already an important place in Roman times.

29757.q: What is the Abbey of Saint-Maurice especially known for?
a: Oldest continuously existing monastery in the West
29757.e: Since it was founded, a religious community has lived at Saint-Maurice without a break. Today it is the Augustinian Canons.
29757.m: Saint-Maurice is seen as the oldest continuously inhabited monastery in the West.

29758.q: What did the monks at Saint-Maurice once do day and night without stopping?
29758.e: The monks took turns in groups, so that singing and prayer in praise of God never stopped. This was called laus perennis.
29758.m: At Saint-Maurice monks once sang and prayed without a break.

29759.q: Which neighbouring country borders the Val Müstair, where St John’s Abbey lies?
29759.e: The Val Müstair lies at the far eastern end of Switzerland. Just after the village of Müstair, South Tyrol begins, which belongs to Italy.
29759.m: Müstair Abbey lies close to the border with Italy.

29761.q: According to tradition, which ruler founded Müstair Abbey?
29761.e: Legend says Charlemagne founded the abbey. A life-size statue of him stands in the church.
29761.m: Charlemagne is seen as the founder of Müstair Abbey.

29762.q: What is the abbey church of Müstair world-famous for?
a: The largest stained-glass windows in Europe
29762.e: Many frescoes with scenes from the Carolingian period survive in the church. There are hardly so many early wall paintings anywhere else.
29762.m: Müstair has unique wall paintings from the Carolingian period.

29763.q: How were experts able to work out the exact founding date of Müstair Abbey?
a: From the tree rings in the building timber
From a coin in the foundations
From an inscription on the doorway
29763.e: Dendrochronology compares the width of the tree rings in wood with known patterns. That way you know when a tree was cut down.
29763.m: Tree rings in wood reveal the age of buildings.

29764.q: Who lives in St John’s Abbey in Müstair today?
29764.e: At first the abbey was a monastery for men. Since the 12th century nuns have lived there following the Rule of St Benedict.
29764.m: Benedictine nuns live in Müstair today.

29765.q: What is housed today in the medieval Planta Tower of Müstair Abbey?
29765.e: The tower was built around 960 and later extended by Abbess Angelina von Planta. Today the abbey museum there shows the history of the abbey.
29765.m: The Planta Tower houses the Müstair Abbey museum.

29766.q: Which hermit lived in the 9th century in the Dark Forest, where Einsiedeln Abbey later grew up?
29766.e: Meinrad was a monk from Reichenau who withdrew into solitude. He is seen as the spiritual founder of Einsiedeln.
29766.m: St Meinrad lived as a hermit where Einsiedeln Abbey later stood.

29767.q: How did the hermit Meinrad die?
29767.e: Two robbers killed Meinrad in 861. Since then he has been honoured as a martyr.

29768.q: According to legend, which animals followed Meinrad’s murderers?
29768.e: The birds gave away the killers, who were then caught. That is why the abbey and the village of Einsiedeln have these animals on their coat of arms.
29768.m: Two ravens are the heraldic animals of Einsiedeln.

29769.q: Which monastic rule do the monks of Einsiedeln Abbey live by?
29769.e: In 934 Eberhard from Strasbourg gathered the hermits into a community following Benedict’s rule. Einsiedeln is still a Benedictine monastery today.

29770.q: Who destroyed the Chapel of Grace in Einsiedeln in 1798?
29770.e: When the French marched into Switzerland in 1798, the chapel got torn down. It got rebuilt from 1815 to 1817.
29770.m: The Chapel of Grace in Einsiedeln was destroyed in 1798 and later rebuilt.

29771.q: In which architectural style was Einsiedeln Abbey rebuilt from 1704?
29771.e: Brother Caspar Moosbrugger planned the huge Baroque complex. The abbey church was consecrated in 1735.
29771.m: Einsiedeln Abbey is a Baroque building.

29772.q: Who attacked Einsiedeln Abbey in January 1314 in the so-called March Dispute?
29772.e: Schwyz and the abbey argued for a long time about pastures and forests. In 1314 men from Schwyz plundered the abbey and took monks prisoner.
29772.m: In the March Dispute, Schwyz and Einsiedeln Abbey fought over land.

29773.q: Through which narrow gorge in the canton of Uri does the route to the Gotthard lead?
29773.e: Only a bridge in the Schöllenen Gorge made the Gotthard route passable. According to legend, the Devil built the Devil’s Bridge.
29773.m: The route to the Gotthard leads through the Schöllenen Gorge.

29774.q: What already stood at the top of the Gotthard Pass in the Middle Ages to take in travellers?
29774.e: A hospice is a simple inn for travellers. On the Gotthard, muleteers and pilgrims found shelter there from cold and storms.
29774.m: On the Gotthard a hospice gave travellers shelter.

29775.q: Which big trading city in northern Italy could traders from the north reach especially directly over the Gotthard?
29775.e: From the Gotthard the route leads down through Ticino into Lombardy. Milan was the most important trading city there.
29775.m: Over the Gotthard you reached Milan directly.

29776.q: What were the men called who took goods over the alpine passes with mules and horses?
29776.e: A pack animal carries loads on its back. The muleteers led such animals in lines over the passes.
29776.m: Muleteers took goods over the passes with pack animals.

29777.q: Which village in Ticino lies on the south side of the Gotthard Pass?
29777.e: From the top of the pass the road leads down to Airolo in the Leventina valley. Andermatt and Göschenen are on the Uri side.
29777.m: Airolo lies on the south side of the Gotthard.

29778.q: Which saint is the Gotthard named after?
29778.e: At the top of the pass stood a chapel for St Godehard, a Bishop of Hildesheim. The name Gotthard comes from his name.
29778.m: The Gotthard bears the name of St Godehard.

29780.q: In the legend, what payment did the Devil demand for building the bridge?
a: the soul of the first to cross
a sack full of gold and silver
half of all the harvests in the valley
29780.e: The Devil wanted the soul of the first creature to cross the bridge. That was his price for the work.
29780.m: The Devil demanded the first soul on the bridge.

29781.q: In the legend, how did the people of Uri trick the Devil?
a: They let an animal cross first
They tore the bridge down at once
They rang all the church bells
29781.e: Instead of a person, the people of Uri sent an animal across the bridge. So the Devil did not get a human soul.
29781.m: The people of Uri sent an animal across the bridge first.

29782.q: In the legend, what is the boulder called that the Devil wanted to hurl at the bridge in anger?
29782.e: According to legend, the Devil was driven away with a cross, and the stone missed the bridge. The Devil’s Stone lies near Göschenen and was moved in the 1970s for road building.
29782.m: The Devil’s Stone recalls the legend of the Devil’s Bridge.

29783.q: Why was the route through the Schöllenen Gorge so dangerous in the past?
a: Because of steep rock walls and the wild Reuss
Because of many robbers in the forest
29783.e: In the narrow gorge the Reuss rushes down between steep rocks. Only bridges and walkways made the route to the Gotthard passable.
29783.m: The Schöllenen is a narrow, wild gorge of the Reuss.

29784.q: What material did people use for the first Devil’s Bridge?
29784.e: The first bridge over the Reuss had been built of wood. Later a stone bridge replaced it.
29784.m: The first Devil’s Bridge: made of wood.

29785.q: Which town did Duke Berthold V of Zähringen found in 1191?
29785.e: Berthold V had the town built on a well-protected site. It later became the most powerful city of the Confederation.
29785.m: Berthold V of Zähringen founded the town of Bern in 1191.

29786.q: According to legend, which animal is Bern named after?
29786.e: According to legend, the first animal Berthold V killed while hunting was a bear. That is why Bern also has a bear on its coat of arms.
29786.m: Bern is said to be named after the bear.

29787.q: What is the name of the fountain in Bern’s old town that remembers the family who founded the city?
29787.e: The fountain remembers the dukes who founded the city. It stands in the Kramgasse and dates from the 16th century.
29787.m: The Zähringer Fountain in Bern remembers the founders of the city.

29788.q: In which year did the House of Zähringen die out with Berthold V?
29788.e: Berthold V had no sons. With his death in 1218 the House of Zähringen came to an end, and his lands were divided up.
29788.m: The House of Zähringen died out in 1218.

29789.q: Which town on the lake of the same name is a Zähringer town?
29789.e: Murten was laid out as a town by the Zähringers in the 12th century. It is one of the Zähringer towns.

29790.q: Why did the Zähringers found new towns?
a: To secure their rule and trade
To build ports for seagoing ships
29790.e: Towns with walls protected roads and river crossings. Markets also brought the lords taxes and tolls.
29790.m: The Zähringers used towns to secure their rule and trade.

29791.q: Where did the Zähringer family originally come from?
29791.e: Zähringen Castle lies near Freiburg im Breisgau. From there the dukes also founded towns in what is now Switzerland.
29791.m: The Zähringers came from southern Germany.

29792.q: In which present-day canton is Kyburg Castle, after which the Counts of Kyburg named themselves?
29792.e: Kyburg Castle lies near Winterthur. The powerful family of counts took its name from this castle.
29792.m: Kyburg Castle is in the canton of Zurich.

29793.q: Which family took over the large lands of the Kyburgs after they died out?
29793.e: The only heiress was a child. Her guardian belonged to this family and brought the inheritance to his house.
29793.m: The Kyburg inheritance went to the Habsburgs.

29794.q: Which future king became the guardian of Anna, the Kyburg heiress?
29794.e: Rudolf’s mother was a Kyburg. As guardian he managed the inheritance, and in 1273 he became King of the Romans.
29794.m: Rudolf of Habsburg managed the Kyburg inheritance.

29795.q: Which town in Central Switzerland was founded by the Kyburgs?
29795.e: Zug lies on Lake Zug and was laid out as a town by the Counts of Kyburg. Later it passed to the Habsburgs.
29795.m: The Kyburgs founded the town of Zug.

29796.q: Which town on the Limmat with hot springs did the Kyburgs found around 1230?
29796.e: Baden was already known in Roman times for its thermal springs. The Kyburgs founded a town there around 1230.
29796.m: Baden was founded by the Kyburgs.

29797.q: Why did the power of the Counts of Kyburg end around 1264?
a: There were no more male heirs
They lost a battle against Bern
29797.e: Hartmann V died in 1263 and Hartmann IV in 1264. After that there were no more male Kyburgs, and the inheritance went to the Habsburgs.

29798.q: What is Kyburg Castle near Winterthur today?
29798.e: Kyburg Castle belongs to the canton of Zurich. In the museum you can find out how people lived in a castle in the Middle Ages.
29798.m: Kyburg Castle is a museum today.

29799.q: What did it mean for an area to have imperial freedom?
a: It was directly under the king
It could choose its own king
It no longer belonged to any empire
29799.e: Areas with imperial freedom had no count or duke above them. They were answerable only to the king or emperor.
29799.m: Areas with imperial freedom were directly under the king.

29800.q: Which of the Forest Cantons was the first to receive a charter of freedom, in 1231?
29800.e: Uri lay on the route to the Gotthard, which was important for the empire. That is why the king took the valley under his direct rule.
29800.m: Uri was the first of the Forest Cantons to receive imperial freedom.

29801.q: Why was Uri particularly important for the king?
a: Because of the route over the Gotthard
29801.e: The route over the Gotthard to Italy ran through Uri. That is why the king took the valley under his direct rule in 1231.
29801.m: Uri was important because of the Gotthard.

29802.q: What did the people of Schwyz receive a charter of freedom from the emperor for in 1240?
a: For a victory in Swiss wrestling
29802.e: Warriors from Schwyz helped Emperor Frederick II during a siege in Italy. As thanks they were granted imperial freedom.
29802.m: Schwyz received its charter for helping in war.

29803.q: Which three places are called the Forest Cantons?
29803.e: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden lie on Lake Lucerne. They received charters of freedom early on and are seen as the core of the Confederation.
29803.m: The Forest Cantons are Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden.

29804.q: Whose rule was Uri freed from by its charter of freedom?
29804.e: Uri had previously been pledged to the Counts of Habsburg. The king bought the valley back and promised never to give it away again.
29804.m: The charter freed Uri from the Habsburgs.

29805.q: In which year was the Pact of Brunnen made?
29805.e: The charter is dated 9 December 1315. It renewed the older alliance of the Forest Cantons.
29805.m: The Pact of Brunnen dates from 1315.

29806.q: According to the Pact of Brunnen, what did the members have to give each other if one was attacked?
29806.e: If one member was attacked, the others had to help. Each member paid the costs of this help itself.
29806.m: In the Pact of Brunnen, the members promised each other help at their own expense.

29807.q: According to the Pact of Brunnen, what was nobody allowed to buy?
29807.e: Judges were not to be able to buy their office. Otherwise rich people could have bent the law to suit themselves.
29807.m: Nobody was allowed to buy the office of judge.

29808.q: Which word for the allies appears for the first time in the charter of Brunnen?
29808.e: The allies were bound to each other by an oath (“Eid”). That is why they called themselves companions of the oath.
29808.m: The word “Eidgenossen” (Confederates) appears for the first time in the Pact of Brunnen.

29809.q: According to the Pact of Brunnen, how were disputes between the members to be settled?
29809.e: Disputes between allies were not to be settled by force. People looked for mediators or went to court.
29809.m: Disputes between the members were settled by mediation and the law.

29810.q: According to the Pact of Brunnen, what was no member allowed to do without the agreement of the others?
29810.e: No member was to place itself under a lord or ally with outsiders on its own. This was meant to keep them united.
29810.m: No member could accept a foreign lord without the others.

29811.e: Brunnen lies in the canton of Schwyz on the shore of Lake Uri. This is part of Lake Lucerne.

29812.q: What title did the head of the town of Lucerne have in the Middle Ages?
29812.e: In Lucerne a Schultheiss (a kind of mayor) led the council. The title also existed in Bern and Solothurn.
29812.m: Lucerne was led by a Schultheiss.

29813.q: Compared with Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden, what was Lucerne in the alliance?
29813.e: The Forest Cantons were rural valley communities. With Lucerne, a town joined the alliance for the first time.
29813.m: Lucerne was the first town in the alliance.

29814.q: Whose rule did Lucerne belong to when it allied itself with the Forest Cantons?
29814.e: Lucerne was under Habsburg rule. The alliance with the Forest Cantons was therefore a brave step for the people of Lucerne.
29814.m: At that time Lucerne belonged to Habsburg.

29815.q: In which year did Lucerne ally itself with Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden?
29815.e: Lucerne made a perpetual alliance with the Forest Cantons in 1332. This brought the first town into the Confederation.

29816.q: How did goods from Lucerne usually travel on towards the Gotthard?
29816.e: There were hardly any roads along the steep lake shore. So goods were taken by boat to Flüelen and from there onwards by pack animals.
29816.m: From Lucerne, goods went by boat towards the Gotthard.

29817.q: Why was Lucerne particularly important for the Forest Cantons?
a: It was their most important market town
It lay right on the Rhine
29817.e: In Lucerne the farmers sold their cattle and bought grain and salt. The town also lay on the Gotthard route.
29817.m: Lucerne was the most important market of the Forest Cantons.

29818.q: Which famous wooden bridge in Lucerne was built around 1365?
29818.e: The Chapel Bridge was part of the town’s fortifications. It is one of the oldest covered wooden bridges in Europe.
29818.m: The Chapel Bridge in Lucerne dates from the 14th century.

29819.q: Which office in Zurich was Rudolf Brun the first to hold, in 1336?
29819.e: After the overthrow of the old council, an assembly elected Brun mayor for life. He was the first mayor of Zurich.
29819.m: Rudolf Brun was the first mayor of Zurich.

29820.q: Which groups got seats on the Zurich council through Rudolf Brun’s constitution?
29820.e: Brun’s guild constitution of 1336 divided the craftsmen into guilds. Their guild masters now sat on the council.
29820.m: Through Brun, the guilds entered the Zurich council.

29821.q: Which group gained a share in governing Zurich through the guild constitution of 1336?
29821.e: Before that, mainly rich merchants and nobles had ruled. Through Brun, the craftsmen entered the council via their guilds.
29821.m: Through Brun, the craftsmen helped govern Zurich.

29822.q: How long was Rudolf Brun to remain mayor of Zurich?
29822.e: After the overthrow of 1336, Brun was elected mayor for life. He ruled until his death in 1360.
29822.m: Rudolf Brun was mayor for life.

29823.q: Which lake is Zurich, the city Rudolf Brun ruled, on?
29823.e: Zurich lies at the lower end of Lake Zurich, where the Limmat flows out. Under Brun the city grew more powerful.

29824.q: With which places did Zurich make its perpetual alliance?
29824.e: Zurich allied itself with the three Forest Cantons and with Lucerne. This made the alliance bigger, reaching as far as the Limmat.
29824.m: Zurich allied itself with the Forest Cantons and Lucerne.

29825.q: In which century did Zurich join the Confederation?
29825.e: Zurich made a perpetual alliance with the Forest Cantons and Lucerne in 1351. That was in the 14th century.

29826.q: Why did Zurich seek an alliance with the Confederates?
a: It wanted to buy the Gotthard
It was looking for a new bishop
29826.e: Mayor Rudolf Brun had had Rapperswil destroyed, which belonged to a branch of the Habsburgs. Zurich therefore needed strong allies.
29826.m: Zurich allied itself with the Confederates against Habsburg.

29827.q: In which year did Bern join the Confederation?
29827.e: On 6 March 1353 Bern made a perpetual alliance. With this the powerful city became part of the Confederation.

29828.q: What number member of the Confederation did Bern become?
29828.e: Before Bern came Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Lucerne, Zurich, Glarus and Zug. Bern was the last of the old members of this period.

29829.q: With which places did Bern make a direct alliance in 1353?
29829.e: Bern allied itself with the three Forest Cantons. It was therefore linked to the other members only through them.
29829.m: In 1353 Bern allied itself with the three Forest Cantons.

29830.q: Why was Bern a particularly important new partner for the Confederates in 1353?
a: Bern was a large and powerful city
29830.e: Even then Bern had a large territory and a strong army. With Bern, the Confederation became much stronger.
29830.m: With Bern, a powerful city joined the alliance.

29831.q: How was Bern linked to Zurich and Lucerne after 1353?
a: Only indirectly through the Forest Cantons
Not at all, they were enemies
29831.e: The alliances of the Confederation were a web of separate treaties. Bern had a charter only with the Forest Cantons.
29831.m: Bern was linked to Zurich and Lucerne only through the Forest Cantons.

29832.q: How did Bern often enlarge its territory in the 14th century?
a: It inherited all of Habsburg’s land
It reclaimed land from Lake Thun
29832.e: Bern bought towns and lordships from nobles in debt, for example Burgdorf and Thun in 1384. This made its territory grow a lot.
29832.m: Bern often enlarged its territory by buying land.

29833.q: Until which year did Brun’s guild constitution essentially remain in force?
29833.e: The guild constitution lasted until the end of the Old Swiss Confederacy. Only the Helvetic Republic brought a new order.

29834.q: Which city won the Battle of Laupen in 1339?
29834.e: On 21 June 1339 Bern and its allies won at Laupen. Afterwards Bern became even more powerful.

29835.q: Which town fought against Bern at Laupen together with many nobles?
29835.e: Fribourg and the nobles of western Switzerland feared Bern’s growing power. That is why they marched against Bern together.
29835.m: Fribourg fought against Bern at Laupen.

29836.q: Who helped Bern in the Battle of Laupen?
29836.e: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden sent warriors to Laupen. Solothurn and some valley communities also helped Bern.
29836.m: The Forest Cantons helped Bern at Laupen.

29837.q: What did Bern’s enemies besiege before the Battle of Laupen?
29837.e: Fribourg and many nobles besieged Laupen. Bern came to help the town with its allies.
29837.m: Bern helped the besieged town of Laupen.

29838.q: Why did Fribourg and many nobles fight against Bern in 1339?
a: Bern wanted to elect a king
29838.e: Bern was becoming bigger and more powerful. Fribourg and the nobles of western Switzerland wanted to stop that.

29839.q: What did the victory at Laupen mean for Bern?
a: Bern could extend its power further
29839.e: After Laupen, Bern became the most important power in the west of what is now Switzerland. Agnes of Hungary negotiated the peace in 1340.
29839.m: After Laupen, Bern became even more powerful.

29840.q: In which battle is Arnold Winkelried said to have sacrificed himself?
29840.e: There the Confederates fought against a Habsburg army of knights. Winkelried’s deed is said to have made their victory possible.
29840.m: Winkelried is said to have sacrificed himself at Sempach.

29841.q: What is Winkelried said to have done in the battle?
a: He warned the army with a horn
29841.e: He is said to have gathered a bundle of lances into his arms and pulled them towards himself. This made a gap in the knights’ front line.
29841.m: Winkelried is said to have grabbed the enemy’s lances.

29842.q: Which place did the Winkelried family come from?
29842.e: The Winkelrieds were a family of knights from Nidwalden. They are recorded in this place from about 1250.

29843.q: What does Winkelried stand for in Swiss memory?
29843.e: Winkelried is said to have given his life so that his comrades could win. That is why he became a model of self-sacrifice.
29843.m: Winkelried is seen as a model of self-sacrifice.

29844.q: What does the famous Winkelried monument in Stans from 1865 show?
a: Winkelried with enemy lances in his arms
Winkelried with a crossbow and an apple
29844.e: The sculptor Ferdinand Schlöth showed Winkelried dying with the knights’ lances. The monument was unveiled in 1865.
29844.m: The Winkelried monument shows him with the enemy’s lances.

29845.q: Why do historians doubt that Winkelried really acted like this?
a: The deed is only mentioned much later
He only lived a hundred years afterwards
He fought on the other side
29845.e: The story first appears in a Zurich chronicle from around 1476, and there still without a name. No earlier source reports it.
29845.m: Winkelried’s deed is only mentioned long after the battle.

29846.q: Which famous sentence does the legend give to Winkelried?
a: “I will open a path for you”
29846.e: The “path” means the gap in the knights’ row of lances. The historian Johannes von Müller put the sentence into these words in 1805.
29846.m: Winkelried is said to have said: “I will open a path for you.”

29847.q: In which year did the Battle of Näfels take place?
29847.e: The battle was on 9 April 1388. Two years after Sempach, the people of Glarus defeated Habsburg.
29847.m: The Battle of Näfels was in 1388.

29848.q: Which place defended itself against Habsburg at Näfels?
29848.e: The people of Glarus wanted to free themselves from Habsburg rule. Supported by a few warriors from Central Switzerland, they won.
29848.m: At Näfels, the people of Glarus defeated Habsburg.

29849.e: Every year the people of Glarus walk in procession to the battle memorial. There the names of those who died are read out.
29849.m: The Näfelser Fahrt remembers the battle every year.

29850.q: In which season does the Näfelser Fahrt take place?
29850.e: The Näfelser Fahrt is on the first Thursday in April. The battle took place in April 1388.
29850.m: The Näfelser Fahrt is in April.

29851.q: Where did the people of Glarus get support from at Näfels?
29851.e: A few warriors from Central Switzerland helped the people of Glarus. Together they defeated the much larger Habsburg army.
29851.m: At Näfels, men from Central Switzerland helped the people of Glarus.

29852.q: Among other things, what did the people of Glarus use to defend themselves against the horsemen?
29852.e: From the slope, the people of Glarus threw stones at the disordered army. Many enemies fled and drowned near Weesen.
29852.m: The people of Glarus threw stones at the enemy horsemen.

29853.q: Roughly how many fighters faced each other at Näfels?
29853.e: The Confederates were heavily outnumbered. Even so, they lost only about 55 men, while the enemy lost around 1,700.
29853.m: At Näfels a small band defeated a much larger army.

29854.q: In which century was the Priests’ Charter (Pfaffenbrief) agreed?
29854.e: The Priests’ Charter was agreed in 1370. The year 1370 belongs to the 14th century.
29854.m: The Priests’ Charter dates from the 14th century.

29855.q: Who is meant by the word “Pfaffen” in the Priests’ Charter (Pfaffenbrief)?
29855.e: “Pfaffe” used to be a word for a priest or clergyman. The charter mainly set out their position.

29856.q: What did the Priests’ Charter lay down for clergymen?
a: They came under the local courts
They were not allowed to buy weapons
29856.e: In worldly disputes, clergymen could no longer appeal to foreign courts. Exceptions applied only to marriage and church matters.
29856.m: Clergymen also had to accept the local courts.

29857.q: What led to the Priests’ Charter in 1370?
29857.e: A Zurich clergyman attacked the Schultheiss of Lucerne and refused to accept a worldly court. After that, the members agreed the Priests’ Charter.
29857.m: An attack by a clergyman led to the Priests’ Charter.

29858.q: Who made the Priests’ Charter to make their territory safer?
29858.e: Zurich, Lucerne, Zug, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden agreed the Priests’ Charter in 1370. It ensured peace on the road to the Gotthard.
29858.m: Several members of the Confederation made the Priests’ Charter.

29859.q: Which route was the Priests’ Charter meant to make particularly safe?
a: The route from Zurich to the Gotthard
The route from Bern to Geneva
The route from Basel to Strasbourg
The route from Chur to Venice
29859.e: The members promised peace on the road from Zurich to the Gotthard. Safe roads were important for trade.
29859.m: The Priests’ Charter protected the route from Zurich to the Gotthard.

29861.q: According to the Sempach Charter, what were the warriors only allowed to do with their captains’ permission?
29861.e: Disorderly plundering put an army in danger. That is why permission from the leaders was needed.
29861.m: Plundering was only allowed with the captains’ permission.

29862.q: According to the Sempach Charter, which buildings were the warriors to spare?
29862.e: Churches and monasteries were not to be attacked or robbed. This applied even in enemy territory.
29862.m: Churches and monasteries had to be spared in war.

29863.e: In 1393 the eight members of the Confederation and Solothurn agreed on this shared set of rules.
29863.m: The Sempach Charter applied to the members of the Confederation.

29864.q: According to the Sempach Charter, which people were to be spared if they were not fighting?
29864.e: The charter banned attacks on women who were not taking part in the fighting. It was an early rule to protect the defenceless.
29864.m: Women who were not fighting had to be spared.

29865.q: According to the Sempach Charter, how was the spoils of war to be shared?
29865.e: Each member was to receive its share of the spoils. This was meant to avoid quarrels between the allies.
29865.m: The spoils were shared out proportionally.

29866.q: Whom did the people of Appenzell fight against at the start of the Appenzell Wars?
